Every single turn represents exactly one second of real-time action.

  • You do not get to move, draw a weapon, and attack all at once.
  • You must choose one primary maneuver to execute during your 1-second window.

Combat order is strictly determined by your Basic Speed secondary attribute (which is derived from your Health and Dexterity).

  • The character with the highest Basic Speed acts first.
  • If there is a tie, the character with the highest Dexterity (DX) goes first.
  • Turn order remains exactly the same every single second; you do not re-roll initiative.

On your second of action, you must choose one maneuver from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.BUSu7dFLs9IzOvPY]{Chapter 9}: Combat Maneuvers & Techniques. The most common combat maneuvers are:

  • Attack: Stand still or step 1 yard, and make a single attack.
  • Move and Attack: Run up to your full movement capability, but your attack is capped at a maximum skill of 9 and you cannot parry.
  • All-Out Attack: Give up your ability to defend yourself entirely for this turn in exchange for massive offensive bonuses (like +4 to hit, +2 damage, or making two attacks instead of one).
  • All-Out Defense: Focus purely on survival, forgoing any offensive action this turn.
  • Do Nothing: Take no action. The only maneuver available to a character who is conscious but stunned or surprised -- see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.BUSu7dFLs9IzOvPY]{Chapter 9} for the Active Defense penalty and recovery roll while stunned.
  • Ready: Draw a weapon, reload a gun, pick an item up off the ground, or re-balance a heavy axe.

Weapon Handling Notes

  • Hands, and What They're Holding: A character can only wield what their hands can hold. A one-handed weapon occupies one hand; a two-handed weapon occupies both.
  • Spotting a two-handed weapon. Its entry carries a † -- in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12} beside the weapon itself, and in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.gxAN3kXd5U4q1H3c]{Chapter 11} beside the Base ST of the Base component it is built on. Rifle, Assault and Carbine Stocks, Heavy Mounts and Harness Tanks all carry it.
  • What two hands allow. A rifle up, or a sword and a blaster, but not a rifle and a sword at once. A species with more or fewer hands scales accordingly.
  • One-Handing a Two-Handed Weapon. You can wield a two-handed (†) weapon in one hand -- at -2 to hit if it is balanced, or -4 if it is Unbalanced (U) -- freeing your other hand for a second weapon. Held this way it handles as Unbalanced: no attacking and parrying in the same turn until your ST reaches 1.5× its Min ST. Strength eases the grip, too: at 1.5× Min ST the to-hit penalty is halved (round toward zero), and at 2× it is gone (see ST, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12}). Damage is unchanged.
  • Everything else is stowed. Slung, sheathed or holstered. Stowed gear costs nothing to carry beyond its weight and cannot be used until drawn, which is a Ready maneuver (see Holsters & Slings, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}, for the Fast-Draw bonus a proper rig gives).
  • Switching weapons costs two actions. Stowing a two-handed weapon and drawing a sidearm is one action each -- which is why a soldier under fire usually drops the rifle on its sling instead.

Combat techniques are an optional set of distinct fighting techniques that represent advanced training in specific combat styles, allowing for powerful effects at the cost of Endurance Points (EP). If your character knows a Combat Technique, you may choose 1 per turn to use in place of a normal attack. The Combat Technique may supersede a chosen maneuver if used.

Lightsaber Forms represent highly specialized schools of combat, each emphasizing different aspects of lightsaber mastery – from defense to offense, agility to raw power, or integration with Force abilities. A Force-sensitive character with Lightsaber Combat skill can learn these forms. Lightsaber forms may be used in conjunction with a combat technique.

  • Choosing or switching a Lightsaber Form takes a Free Action at the start of your turn. You can only have one form active at a time. You cannot switch forms in the middle of a turn.
  • When used in conjunction with a combat technique, if a form is not already active, you activate your form, and choose 1 learned combat technique to use during your turn in place of a normal attack/ damage roll.

Dual Wielding Weapons

A character may wield a weapon in both (or multiple if more than 2) hands. This results in a -4 penalty to hit and a -1 penalty to parry with your (or each) off-hand (non dominant) weapon unless the character has the Ambidexterity advantage, or is using a lightsaber form that incorporates Jar’Kai. Dual Wielding allows you to make two (or more if multi-limbed) attacks in a single turn using an Attack, All-Out Attack maneuver, or Combat Technique.

Which Hand Is Dominant: Every character names one hand as dominant at creation. It costs nothing, it never changes in play, and it is the hand the off-hand penalties are measured against -- without it there is no way to say which weapon takes the -4. Right is the default for a standard humanoid; a player may name the left instead at no cost, and a species whose limbs are not paired names whichever appendage it habitually leads with. A character with more than two hands still names exactly one dominant: a four-armed Besalisk with a blade in each hand strikes at full skill with one and at -4 with the other three, because dexterity of that kind is trained, not issued with the limb. A character with one hand has that hand as dominant and no off-hand penalty to worry about, having nothing to put in the other.

Ambidexterity and Dominance: Ambidexterity does not remove your dominant hand -- it removes the penalty for not using it. The designation stays on the sheet and keeps mattering anywhere else handedness is asked about (which hand a Fast-Draw comes from, which arm a cripple result lands on, which hand is free after a two-handed weapon is stowed); it simply stops costing you -4 to hit and -1 to parry. A four-armed character with Ambidexterity fights at full skill with all four.

When you attack an opponent, SoTMW uses a “success and defense” system rather than an Armor Class system. Every attack requires four distinct steps:

Step 1: The Attack Roll (3d6)

You roll three six-sided dice against your weapon skill (e.g., Broadsword-14).

  • You must roll equal to or lower than your skill level to succeed.
  • Modifiers apply here, such as penalties for aiming at a specific hit location (like the eyes or limbs) or bad lighting.

Step 2: The Active Defense Roll (3d6)

If your attack succeeds, your opponent gets a chance to completely avoid it. They do not roll against a skill, but rather one of their Active Defenses:

  • Dodge: Based on Basic Speed: floor(Basic Speed) + 3, then Combat Reflexes (+1) and encumbrance (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}). Used to jump out of the way.
  • Parry: Based on weapon skill. Used to deflect the blow with a weapon.
  • Block: Based on Shield skill. Used to catch the blow on a shield.
  • If the defender rolls equal to or lower than their defense score, they take zero damage. This is where they might spend 1 EP on Feverish Defense to get a crucial +2 to their odds. (Feverish Defense: spend 1 EP before rolling to gain +2 on a single active defense roll.)

Step 3: Damage Bases

Before determining damage types, physical melee and thrown weapon damage is calculated using one of two mechanical bases found on the ST Damage Table:

  • thr (Thrust): Straight-pushing, poking, or stabbing attacks (e.g., spears, punches). Generally yields fewer dice but allows high-multiplier damage types.
  • sw (Swing): Leveraged, swinging strikes using a weapon’s centrifugal force (e.g., axes, swords). Generally yields significantly more raw dice than thrusting.

Unarmed Strikes: A punch, a kick, an elbow or a headbutt is a Thrust attack off your own ST, read straight from the ST Damage Table with no modifier -- a character at ST 12 punches for 1d-1, a Gorax at ST 45 for 5d. Unarmed damage is crushing unless something changes the type (see Sharp Claws, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.2I6Edey1uD2bgyES]{Chapter 4}). Punches and kicks deal the same damage; what separates them is what can raise it. Striking ST reaches both. Arm ST reaches the punch and not the kick, because a kick is not an arm action (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}). Foot-mounted hardware is the kick's own route -- a Myomer Boost installed in a Foot, or the Aratech “Strider” Bionic Foot, each add +1 damage on kicks (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}). Training raises it too: striking with Karate (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}) adds +1 per die of thrust damage at Karate DX+1, and +2 per die at DX+2 or higher, on punches and kicks alike. Karate alone among the unarmed skills carries this bonus -- Brawling, Judo, Echani Martial Arts and Teräs Käsi strike at base thrust damage.

When making a ranged attack (Guns, Bow, Thrown Weapon, etc.), your base skill is modified by the weapon’s stats and external conditions. Calculate your effective skill using these steps:

  • Acc (Accuracy): If you take the Aim maneuver for at least 1 turn, add the weapon’s Acc bonus to your skill roll. Aiming for consecutive turns grants an additional +1 (2 turns) or +2 (3+ turns). Attached scopes or targeting lasers add their own bonuses here.
  • Bulk: A negative modifier reflecting the weapon’s size and clumsiness. Bulk is subtracted from your skill if you try to attack after a Move and Attack maneuver, or if you use the weapon in close combat.
  • Recoil (Rcl): Determines how easy it is to land multiple shots during a rapid-fire burst. For every full multiple of Rcl your attack roll succeeds by, you score one additional hit (up to the maximum number of shots fired).

Size and Speed/Range

Distance, target size, and target speed are grouped into a unified progression modifier.

  • Range & Speed Penalty: Consult the Size and Speed/Range Table using the target’s distance in yards. Common penalties include:
  • 2 yards: -1
  • 3 yards: -2
  • 5 yards: -3
  • 7 yards: -4
  • 10 yards: -5
  • 15 yards: -6
  • 20 yards: -7
  • 30 yards: -8
  • 50 yards: -9
  • 100 yards: -11
  • Target Size Modifier (SM): Add the target’s Size Modifier to your roll. Human standard is SM 0. A larger target (e.g., a car or giant at SM +2) makes the attack easier (+2 skill), while a smaller target (e.g., a rat at SM -6) makes it harder (-6 skill).

Step 4: Damage

If the defender fails their active defense, the blow lands. Depending on the blow, the character takes one of the following kinds of damage:

1. Physical & Melee Types

  • cr (Crushing)
  • Blunt impact like fists, clubs, or falls.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • cut (Cutting)
  • Edged weapons like swords, axes, or vibroblades.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.5.
  • imp (Impaling)
  • Piercing weapons like spears, daggers, or arrows.
  • Wounding multiplier: x2.

2. Piercing Sub-Types

  • pi- (Small Piercing)
  • Needle-like punctures or tiny bullets.
  • Wounding multiplier: x0.5.
  • pi (Piercing)
  • Standard firearms and slugthrowers.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • pi+ (Large Piercing)
  • Large caliber rounds or hollow points.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.5.
  • pi++ (Huge Piercing)
  • Massive anti-materiel rounds and anti-vehicular slugs.
  • Wounding multiplier: x2.

3. Energy & Exotic Types

  • burn (Burning)
  • Fire, lasers, and thermal plasma.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Sets flammable targets on fire.
  • cor (Corrosive)
  • Acid or disintegration that destroys DR.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Permanently erodes target DR per 5 points of basic damage dealt.
  • tox (Toxic)
  • Poisons, biological agents, and cellular toxins.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Has no effect on machines, droids, or unliving constructs.
  • end (Endurance Damage)
  • Cryo-attacks, freeze rays, environmental temperature drains, Force-based life drain, and other endurance-sapping effects.
  • Wounding multiplier: N/A (Drains EP directly instead of HP).
  • sonic (Sonic / Acoustic)
  • High-frequency sound waves and localized acoustic shockwaves.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Ignores non-sealed physical DR (bypasses armor unless it is sound-dampened or vacuum-sealed). Any hit that inflicts penetrating damage forces an immediate HT roll (minus penetrating damage) to avoid physical stunning and temporary deafness.
  • ion (Ionization / EMP)
  • Ion streams, EMP pulses, and particle charges targeting electronic pathways.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1 vs. droids/electronics (drains PP — see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}’s Power Points system, mechanically distinct from EP loss — not HP directly); x0.5 EP damage vs. living flesh.
  • Special: x2 vs energy shields. And temporarily disables unshielded target electronic systems, electronic weapons, armor, or starship avionics.
  • shock (True Shock)
  • Pure electrical currents and arc discharges targeting living nerve paths.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Bypasses conductive metallic armor (DR 0 vs. shock). Any penetrating hit forces an immediate HT roll (minus penetrating damage) to avoid physical stunning and falling prone.
  • stun (Stun / Non-Lethal)
  • Subduing energy bolts, neural disruptors, and stun blasters.
  • Wounding multiplier: N/A (Does not inflict direct HP wounds).
  • Special: Reduces target Endurance Points (EP) or forces an HT roll (minus damage) to avoid immediate incapacitation or unconsciousness.
  • energy (Raw Energy)
  • Coherent force blasts, particle beams, and raw plasma/Force strikes. Blaster bolts, lightsaber blades, and Force lightning are all energy damage.
  • Wounding multiplier: x1.
  • Special: Pure kinetic/Force energy beam. Ignores heat and cold environmental protections and does not ignite fires or trigger incendiary hazards.

Mechanical Interactions & Modifiers Note

  • shock vs. sur: shock handles biological nerve disruption and stun rolls on living tissue, whereas sur (Surge) is the innate attack modifier applied to overload circuitry or affect targets with the Electrical disadvantage. An electrical attack can be written as shock or shock, sur depending on whether it affects biological nervous systems, electronic systems, or both.
  • ion vs. sur: ion damage is a primary energy category that specifically targets mechanical/electronic targets (dealing direct HP/PP damage to droids while sparing living tissue), while sur is a secondary attack modifier that forces a short-circuit check.

4. Special & Rule-Breaking Types

  • spec (Special)
  • Damage defined entirely by custom scenario or weapon rules.
  • sub (Substitution)
  • Replaces one specific target stat or attribute with another upon impact.

5. Innate Attack Damage Modifiers

These are specific enhancements or limitations applied to built attacks to change their physical behavior:

  • div (Armor Divisor)
  • Divides target’s DR by (2), (3), (5), or (10).
  • Ignores armor entirely if configured as cosmic.
  • ex (Explosion)
  • An attack marked ex detonates rather than striking normally. Two effects follow: the blast, and — if fragmentation dice are listed — fragmentation, layered on top of it.
  • Direct Hits: a target directly struck by the explosive takes the full listed damage — roll to hit, apply DR, apply the location's wounding modifier, same as any other attack.
  • Tamped/Shaped Charge: a charge braced against a surface or structure to focus the blast. ×1.4 damage.
  • Contained Charge: a charge fully enclosed by the target (smothering a grenade, a charge sealed inside a held container). Use maximum possible damage.
  • Internal Explosion: the charge detonates inside the target (swallowed, or delivered by an attack that already penetrated DR). Treat as a hit to the Vitals (×3 wounding, ×4 if the location is the Head); DR does not apply.
  • Blast (Collateral) Damage: anyone in the blast radius who wasn't the direct target still takes damage, reduced by distance. Safe Distance = 2 × the dice of damage, in yards — beyond that, no blast damage at all.
  • Within Safe Distance: roll the full damage, then divide the result by (3 × distance in yards), rounding down. Apply DR normally against the reduced total, using Torso DR by default (a GM wanting more granularity can roll a random Hit Location instead). Distance is measured in a straight line, height included -- a character three yards above a grenade and four yards to the side of it is five yards from it, not four.
  • Example: a 6d explosion at 4 yards — roll 6d (say, 21), divide by (3 × 4 = 12): 21 ÷ 12 = 1 point of damage before DR.
  • Vacuum: divide by (10 × distance) instead of (3 × distance) — no atmosphere to carry the shockwave. Applies to open space, starship exteriors, and depressurized compartments.
  • Underwater: divide by distance in yards only (no ×3 multiplier) — water transmits a shockwave far more efficiently than air.
  • No active defense applies against the blast itself — you can't Parry or Block a shockwave — but Dodge and Drop (gaining a yard, or reaching cover) still helps before it resolves.
  • frag (Fragmentation)
  • Some explosives list a fragmentation value in brackets (e.g., “6d cr ex [2d]”) — a secondary effect layered onto the blast, representing shrapnel or flying debris.
  • Range: fragmentation is dangerous out to (5 × frag dice) yards — noticeably farther than the blast itself. A [2d] fragmentation pattern threatens everyone within 10 yards.
  • The direct target automatically takes one additional hit of fragmentation damage on top of the blast — no roll to hit required.
  • Everyone else in range takes a single roll of fragmentation damage — cutting (cut), unless the weapon states otherwise. Cover blocks it if the target is actually shielded from the blast; Dodge and Drop is the only other mitigation.
  • Incidental fragmentation: a detonation near loose or breakable material (rubble, scrap metal, broken viewport glass) may inflict a small fragmentation effect even if none is listed — 1d-4 for packed earth, up to 1d for loose scrap metal, at the GM's discretion.

  • inc (Incendiary)
  • Sets flammable targets on fire.
  • Adds burning effects to non-burning damage types.
  • rad (Radiation)
  • Inflicts toxic damage as a radiation dose.
  • Tracked via rads or long-term fatigue instead of immediate physical HP loss.
  • sur (Surge)
  • Overloads electronics and sparks power grids.
  • Short-circuits targets with the Electrical disadvantage or droids/cyborgs.

Environmental & Situational Attack Modifiers

  • Malfunction (Malf.): If your raw 3d6 attack roll matches or exceeds the weapon’s Malf. rating, the weapon jams, misfires, or breaks. A weapon in Fine condition is Malf 17, widening by 1 for each quarter of its Durability lost -- see Malfunctions (Malf) later in this chapter for the full rule.
  • Darkness & Visibility: Penalties range from -1 for dim light, to -9 for total darkness (blind fighting).
  • Pop-Up Attacks: Attacking around a corner or out of cover and immediately hiding again incurs a flat -2 penalty and prevents you from using the Aim maneuver.

Applying Damage

  • Roll Damage: The attacker rolls their weapon’s damage dice (determined by their Strength).
  • Apply DR: Subtract the defender’s Armor value (DR) from the raw damage. If you do 10 points of damage against DR 6 plate armor, only 4 points of “penetrating damage” get through.
  • Apply Wounding Modifiers: Depending on the damage type (Cutting, Impaling, Piercing, Crushing), the damage that penetrates the armor is multiplied. For example, cutting damage is multiplied by x1.5, turning those 4 points into 6 points of actual Hit Point (HP) loss.

Hit Locations

Hit locations determine where a character takes damage, and how difficult it is to deal damage to a part of the body. In cases where a character is missing appendages, either due to their biology, or amputation, the hit location may not be declared as a target for attack and can be treated as no longer a part of the table. This can be reversed by either growing (or regrowing/ reattaching) the limb and becomes a target for attack once again as the table declares.

Extra Limbs, Cybernetics, and Non-Human Hit Locations

When dealing with characters who possess non-standard physiologies—such as extra organic limbs, mechanical appendages, cybernetic prosthetics, or multiple heads—the standard GURPS Hit Location table requires minor adjustments. This guide outlines how to handle both randomized strikes and intentional targeted attacks against these unique anatomical features.

1. Randomized Striking

When an attacker rolls randomly on the Hit Location table (using 3d) against a target with extra limbs, do not rewrite the base roll probabilities. Instead, use the Sub-Location Method to keep combat fast and mathematically consistent.

  • Roll the standard 3d on the Hit Location table.
  • If the result indicates a limb category where the target has extra appendages (e.g., Arms on a 7 or 8, Legs on a 12), roll a subsequent “sub-location” die (typically 1d) to determine which specific limb is hit.
Multi-Limb Allocation Templates
  • Four-Armed Biomorph (Two Left, Two Right):
  • A roll of 7 (Right Arm) or 8 (Left Arm) triggers a 1d roll: 1-3 hits the Upper Arm, 4-6 hits the Lower Arm.
  • Quadruped / Centauroid (Four Legs):
  • A roll of 12 (Legs) triggers a 1d roll: 1-3 hits a Front Leg, 4-6 hits a Hind Leg. Roll a quick odd/even flip (or 1d: odd for Left, even for Right) to determine the exact side.
  • Multi-Headed Beast:
  • A roll of 3-4 (Skull) or 5 (Face) triggers a 1d roll to determine which head takes the impact (e.g., 1-3 for Head A, 4-6 for Head B).
2. Intentional Targeted Attacks (Called Shots)

When a fighter makes a deliberate, targeted attack against a specific extra appendage, cybernetic limb, or non-human anatomical feature, they must accept a penalty to their skill roll.

Base Target Penalties

3. Detailed Mechanics & Modifier Explanations

To ensure these rules integrate smoothly with GURPS tactical combat, keep the following detailed guidelines in mind:

Size Modifier (SM) Adjustments for Appendages

The base penalties assume the target character is Size Modifier 0 and their limbs are proportional. If the target has a non-standard SM, or if a specific limb is disproportionately large or small, adjust the targeting penalty using the relative SM of the limb:

  • Large Appendages: If an extra limb is larger than a human limb (such as a giant’s third arm or a massive hydraulic loading crane arm on a cyborg), reduce the penalty. Find the SM of the limb itself and add it to the base penalty. For example, targeting a massive crane arm (SM +1) reduces the target penalty from -2 to -1.
  • Tiny Appendages: Conversely, if targeting a miniature servo-arm (SM -3), add the negative SM to the penalty, making it significantly harder to hit (e.g., -2 base penalty + (-3) = -5 to hit).
Strikers vs. Extra Limbs

It is critical to distinguish between an Extra Arm and a Striker (such as a scorpion tail, heavy horns, or a spiked elbow blade):

  • Extra Arms are targeted at -2. If crippled, the character loses the ability to hold weapons, climb, or manipulate objects with that arm, but they do not lose any passive combat capability.
  • Strikers are targeted at -3. They are typically denser, harder to hit, and more heavily armored than standard limbs. If an opponent targets your Striker and you fail your active defense, they are attempting to neutralize your primary natural weapon. Crippling a Striker prevents you from using it to attack.
Crippling Thresholds for Multi-Limbed Characters

In standard GURPS, a limb is crippled if it takes major damage exceeding HP/2 in a single blow. However, when a creature or cyborg possesses more than the standard number of limbs, their body distributes structural integrity differently:

  • 3 or 4 Arms/Legs: The damage required to cripple any single limb is reduced to more than HP/3 (round up).
  • 5 or more Arms/Legs: The damage required to cripple any single limb is reduced to more than HP/4 (round up).

Example: A 12-HP cyborg with four mechanical legs has a crippling threshold of more than 4 damage (12/3 = 4) for any individual leg, rather than the standard 6 damage (12/2 = 6).

Cybernetic & Prosthetic Hit Location Special Rules

Targeting a cybernetic limb or component introduces unique tactical options and vulnerabilities. For comprehensive details on purchasing implants, installation risks, system flaws, and repair costs, see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}: Implants & Cybernetics.

  • Localized Damage Resistance & Degradation: Cybernetic limbs feature their own innate DR that stacks with worn armor on that location. However, unlike organic limbs, this DR degrades under stress (losing 1 point of DR for every full 5 points of basic damage rolled against it). If DR reaches 0, the limb is completely destroyed.
  • Electrical Vulnerability: If a cybernetic limb or sensory implant is targeted and hit by an attack with the Electrical surge modifier (such as Ion or EMP weaponry), the user must roll HT. On a failure, the system deactivates or paralyzes the affected area for 1d minutes.
  • Prosthetic “Bleeding” & Fluid Leaks: While cybernetic limbs do not bleed blood, severe structural damage can rupture hydraulic lines, battery units, or coolant channels. Treat this fluid loss as “bleeding” using standard rules, but the HT rolls to stop the leaking must be rolled against Mechanic (Droids) or Armoury (Cybernetics) instead of Physician or First Aid.

Targeting Equipment (Sunder)

A fighter can deliberately strike a weapon, shield, or tool held in an opponent’s hands. This is treated as a specialized called shot.

  • Targeting Held Items: Attacking a held item incurs a flat -4 skill penalty to the attack roll.
  • Resolving the Attack: If the attacker hits and the defender fails their Active Defense, the damage is applied directly to the item. Look up the item’s classification to find its Base DR on the table below:

Facing

A character occupies one hex and faces one of its six hexsides. This splits the six hexes touching them into three arcs relative to that facing: the hex directly ahead plus the two diagonally ahead (Front, 3 hexes), the two hexes directly to the left and right (Side, 2 hexes), and the single hex directly behind (Rear, 1 hex).

Front: Full active defense -- Dodge, Parry, and Block are all available normally.

Side: Dodge and Parry are available normally, but Block is not -- a shield or deflecting tool can’t be brought to bear against an angle the defender isn’t squared up to.

Rear: No active defense of any kind. An attack from the Rear arc is what the Flanked condition (certain traits and creature abilities grant bonus damage against a Flanked target) refers to -- Side attacks do not count as Flanked, only Rear ones.

Changing Facing: A character may change facing once per round, freely, as part of any action that round.

Attacking and Facing: You may attack any target in your Front arc, melee or ranged, with no facing penalty. A target in your Side or Rear arc cannot be attacked until you turn to bring it into your Front arc, which is the free facing change above. Since that change happens once per round, turning to engage one enemy is what exposes your Rear to another -- that trade is the whole point of tracking facing, and it is the reason a lone fighter surrounded by three opponents is in serious trouble even before anyone rolls.

Facing Does Not Change Damage: An attack from the Side or Rear does normal damage and rolls hit location normally. The arc's entire effect is on the defender's active defenses, and losing Block -- or losing all defense -- is already a severe penalty; stacking a damage bonus on top would make a single flank instantly lethal and reduce combat to a positioning race. Traits that key on the Rear arc, such as Sneak Attack, supply their own bonus damage and are the intended way for position to increase harm.

Armor Does Not Care Which Way You Face: A Piece's DR applies equally in every arc. Armor covers the body, not a direction, and tracking front and back DR separately would double the bookkeeping of @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13} for no cinematic gain. A character in Beskar is as protected from behind as in front -- they simply cannot dodge, parry or block the blow.

Wide Fields of View: Peripheral Vision (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.2I6Edey1uD2bgyES]{Chapter 4}, 15 points) shifts every arc one step toward the front: the Side arc counts as Front, and the Rear arc counts as Side (Dodge and Parry, no Block). A character with it is never Flanked. 360-Degree Vision (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.2I6Edey1uD2bgyES]{Chapter 4} or @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}, 25 points) treats every arc as Front -- full active defense in all six hexes, never Flanked, and no facing change is needed to attack in any direction. Both traits leave damage and hit location untouched, as above.

Combat in the KOTOR era is brutal and unforgiving. While shields and armor offer protection, the flesh underneath remains vulnerable. The following mechanics detail how living beings suffer and react to injury in this gritty setting.

Equipment Damage in Combat

Gear does not last forever in a war zone. Blasters overheat, vibroswords clash with lightsabers, and armor buckles under heavy ordnance. The following rules dictate how equipment degrades through the universal condition states (Fine > Damaged > Broken > Destroyed) during active encounters.

The Four Condition States The transition between states happens automatically when an item’s Durability threshold is breached in combat.

  • Fine: The item is in optimal condition. It functions exactly as written at its baseline statistics.
  • Damaged: The item has suffered structural stress, overheating, or component misalignment. A weapon's Malfunction range widens as its Durability falls -- see Malfunctions (Malf) below for the graduated thresholds. For armor and shields specifically, see Armor and Clothing Degradation below. A utility or electronic device -- a belt, gadget, implant, or power pack -- has no attack roll to widen and no worn DR to shed, so a Damaged one keeps working but at -1 to whatever bonus or effect it grants, until repaired; it fails outright only at Broken.
  • Broken: The item is completely inoperable and requires significant overhaul. Weapons cannot fire, strike, or parry. Armor provides 0 DR, and environmental seals fail. Utility devices deactivate instantly.
  • Destroyed (Scrap): The item’s structural integrity or delicate internal circuitry is permanently ruined. It can never be repaired and is stripped of all modification slots. It can only be broken down for raw materials using standard salvaging rules.

Weapon Damage Thresholds A weapon’s Durability (Dur) is tested anytime it is the direct target of an attack or sustains a “Hard Hit” (an attack roll that exceeds the defender’s active defense by a significant margin, e.g., 5+).

Subtract the item’s Dur from the basic penetrating damage rolled by the attacker:

  • 1 to 10 points: The item is stressed. It instantly drops to Damaged, and its Dur is reduced by 1 until repaired (if not destroyed), this is additive.
  • 11 to 19 points: The item becomes Broken.
  • 20+ points: The item is Destroyed if the damage came from a cutting weapon (like a vibroblade), a lightsaber, or an explosive shaped charge; from any other source it is Broken.

Armor and Clothing Degradation: What the character wears takes a beating when in combat.

  • DR Reduction: When the amount of damage dealt to a character is more than the overall DR of their armor, and the character takes HP damage, the armor’s current DR is reduced by 1 (cumulative). This tracked loss is the entire effect of an ordinary hit — it does not additionally trigger the Damaged state’s flat -25% DR reduction (round down).
  • Condition Shifts: A piece’s condition is simply a label read off its current DR: at or above its listed DR, it’s Fine; below listed DR (from the tracking above), it’s Damaged; at 0, it’s Broken. Any further hits to Broken armor render it Destroyed.
  • Major Wounds: Whenever a character suffers a Major Wound (damage from a single blow equal to or greater than half their total HP) on a location protected by armor, that armor immediately drops one full condition step — unlike the gradual tracking above, this applies the new condition’s effect directly (Damaged: DR reduced by a flat 25%, round down; Broken: DR 0), if that’s worse than its current tracked DR. Ordinary hits and Major Wounds never both apply to the same point of damage.
  • Clothing: All clothing has 0 DR, but 10 Dur and follows the same degradation rules as armor, except the Dur is used in the place of DR.

Lightsaber Parry Rules Lightsabers effortlessly slice through mundane materials. Anytime a melee weapon lacking pure Beskar, Phrikite Plating, or a Cortosis Weave attempts to Parry a lightsaber blade (or is parried by one), the defender must immediately roll 3d6 against the weapon’s Dur (plus any energy damage resistance if applicable).

Other lightsabers are exempt unless the hilt is targeted.

  • Success: The weapon survives the clash but instantly becomes Damaged.
  • Failure: The weapon is sheared clean in half and is Destroyed.

Malfunctions (Malf) Blasters and slugthrowers can jam when pushed to their limits in the mud and dust of war, and a damaged blade or blunt weapon may not deal damage effectively even when a hit lands.

  • Baseline Malfunction: A weapon in Fine condition has Malf 17. If an attacker rolls a natural 17 or 18 on their 3d6 Attack Roll, the attack fails regardless of effective skill: a melee weapon is blunted, warped, or its grip slips, dealing half damage rounded up; a ranged weapon or lightsaber misfires, jams, or fails to ignite. Note that at Malf 17 the malfunction range and the critical-failure range (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.QD9SOsp2PLsi7llq]{Chapter 1}: a natural 17 or 18 always fails, and is a critical failure at effective skill 15 or below) are the same two numbers -- an undamaged weapon only ever malfunctions on a roll that was already a critical failure, so in practice Malf costs a Fine weapon nothing extra. It matters as the weapon wears: every step of Malf below 17 catches a roll that would otherwise have been an ordinary miss.
  • Wear Widens the Range: A weapon's Malf drops by 1 for each quarter of its Durability it has lost, so damage degrades reliability gradually rather than in a single step.
  • At 76-100% of listed Dur remaining it is Malf 17
  • at 51-75%, Malf 16
  • at 26-50%, Malf 15
  • at 1-25%, Malf 14
  • at 0 Dur it is Broken and does not function at all.
  • Example: A Dur 13 vibrosword is therefore Malf 17 down to Dur 10, Malf 16 from 9 to 7, Malf 15 from 6 to 4, and Malf 14 from 3 to 1. Round the thresholds down.
  • Damaged Status: A weapon is Damaged the moment it drops below its listed Dur, as described above, but being Damaged is no longer a single flat penalty -- a lightly scuffed blade and one hanging together by its last point of Dur are not equally likely to fail.
  • Armor & Clothing: Clothing and armor use their DR the same way where a GM needs a reliability roll for a sealed suit or powered piece; ordinary armor has no attack roll to fail, and its wear is already tracked as DR loss.
  • Quick Reference: Dur remaining 76-100% = Malf 17 · 51-75% = Malf 16 · 26-50% = Malf 15 · 1-25% = Malf 14 · 0 = Broken. Take the percentage of listed Dur still remaining, round it down, then read the band. Worked examples at common Durabilities -- Dur 10: Malf 17 at 8-10, 16 at 6-7, 15 at 3-5, 14 at 1-2. Dur 13: Malf 17 at 10-13, 16 at 7-9, 15 at 4-6, 14 at 1-3. Dur 16: Malf 17 at 13-16, 16 at 9-12, 15 at 5-8, 14 at 1-4. Dur 20: Malf 17 at 16-20, 16 at 11-15, 15 at 6-10, 14 at 1-5.

Clearing Jams in Combat Mending a standard malfunction in the heat of battle requires a character to take a 1-second Ready maneuver and pass an unmodified skill check corresponding to the weapon: Armoury or Guns (matching the jammed weapon’s specialty), Armstech or Armoury (Melee Weapons), or Lightsaber Construction (Lightsabers).

  • Success: The malfunction is fixed, the jam is cleared, and the weapon can be used/re-ignited on the next turn.
  • Failure: The weapon remains jammed or unable to ignite.
  • Critical Failure: The internal power cell shorts out or a mechanical component violently warps, dropping the weapon’s status directly to Broken.

Cybernetic & Droid Damage Conditions

Characters with cybernetic limbs or fully robotic bodies react differently to damage than flesh and blood. Lacking a traditional nervous system and blood vessels, they ignore several organic vulnerabilities but introduce unique mechanical risks.

I. No Shock Penalties and Major Wounds Damage to a mechanical limb or a droid chassis does not inflict a Shock Penalty, as mechanical constructs do not feel pain. However, they are still vulnerable to sudden, massive trauma representing structural shock or system disruption.

  • Major Wounds: If a droid or a heavily cybernetic character takes damage in a single blow equal to or greater than half their total HP, they suffer a Major Wound. They must immediately roll against HT to avoid stunning or shutdown, just as organics do to avoid unconsciousness.
  • Malfunctions: The player must roll on the Droid Critical Malfunction Table. High rolls can result in a Core Overload, immediate loss of Power Points (PP), internal fires, or force an immediate HT-5 roll to avoid total shutdown, regardless of the initial damage multiplier.

II. Fluid Leaks and Power Drain Droids and cybernetics do not bleed blood. Instead, crippling strikes rupture fluid lines, lubricants, and coolant channels.

  • The Trigger: Whenever a mechanical limb or chassis suffers a Crippling Injury, the character must immediately make a HT roll. On a failure, they begin to leak.
  • The Drain: Instead of losing HP, the character loses 5 Power Points (PP) per interval. This represents the loss of vital fluids forcing the power core to work harder, leading to an accelerated shutdown rather than physical death. The interval is every 10 seconds in combat, or every 1 minute out of combat.
  • Stabilization: The leak stops naturally if the character achieves three consecutive successful HT rolls. Alternatively, it can be patched instantly with a successful Mechanic or Armoury roll and the appropriate tools.

III. Head and Processor Hits Droids and cybernetic brains rely on central processors rather than organic brain tissue.

  • Damage Multipliers: Hits to a droid’s “head” (if it has one) or main chassis that penetrate DR usually only carry a x2 multiplier (rather than the organic x4), unless specifically targeting a volatile component like a power core.
  • Wound Checks: Despite the reduced multiplier, penetrating head hits still trigger Major Wound checks.

IV. Crippling and Amputation Cybernetic limbs are subject to the exact same crippling and amputation thresholds as organic limbs.

  • Limbs (Arms, Legs, Motive Struts): Crippled if the location takes damage over 1/2 HP in a single blow.
  • Extremities (Hands, Feet, Manipulators): Crippled if the location takes damage over 1/3 HP in a single blow.
  • Mechanical parts do not heal. A crippled mechanical limb or extremity is rendered “broken” and remains non-functional until repaired. Use Mechanic, Engineer or Armoury with the specialty that matches what was damaged -- Cybernetics for an implant or prosthetic, Droids for a droid's own limb.
  • Modifications: If a mechanical limb is crippled (takes over 1/2 HP), any modifications installed within that limb are temporarily disabled or jammed.
  • Repairs: A crippled or amputated mechanical limb requires mechanical repair (using skills like Mechanic or Armoury), to restore function.

V. Ionization and EMP Vulnerability Due to their electrical nature, droids and unshielded cybernetic implants are highly vulnerable to ion blasters, EMP grenades, and localized electrical surges.

  • When struck by a weapon with an electrical or ion surge effect, the mechanical target takes its standard damage.
  • Regardless of the damage penetrating DR, the target must immediately make a HT roll. On a failure, the droid or cybernetic limb is completely paralyzed or deactivated for a set duration (typically 1d minutes).

VI. Integrated Cybernetics & Modifications: Installed modifications (e.g., hidden blasters, micro-jets, cyber-jacks) are not treated as separate, targetable hit locations. Equipment is considered integrated into the body part that houses it.

  • Crippling Hits: If a cybernetic limb is crippled (takes over 1/2 HP), any modifications installed within that limb are temporarily disabled or jammed.
  • Destruction: If a body part takes twice the HP needed to cripple it, or drops to negative HP, the limb is completely destroyed. All modifications housed within it are permanently destroyed.
  • Precision Criticals: If an attacker rolls a Critical Hit on a droid or cyborg’s Torso/Chassis, the GM may rule that the attack bypassed outer armor and specifically pierced an Internal Slot, damaging a built-in modification, tool, or vital system.

When a combatant scores a critical success on an attack roll (a natural 3 or 4, or a 5/6 depending on effective skill), the attack lands perfectly and the target gets no Active Defense. Furthermore, the attacker rolls 3d6 and consults the appropriate table below to determine the devastating effects of the blow.

Shock Penalties

GURPS rewards striking first because getting hurt instantly penalizes your next turn. The immediate pain of a wound momentarily impairs a character’s ability to react. Whenever an organic character takes damage, they suffer a Shock Penalty on their next turn.

  • This penalty applies to all DX (Dexterity) and IQ (Intelligence) based skill rolls.
  • The penalty is equal to the points of HP lost, up to a maximum of -4.
  • This penalty lasts only until the end of the character’s next turn.

Major Wounds

A sudden, massive impact can shock the system, causing a combatant to drop their guard or even collapse.

  • A Major Wound occurs when a character takes damage in a single blow equal to or greater than 1/2 their total HP.
  • Upon taking a Major Wound, the character must immediately roll against their HT (Health).
  • Failure: The character is stunned and knocked prone. They must roll HT at the end of each subsequent turn to recover from the stun.
  • Critical Failure: The character falls unconscious.

Crippling Injuries

Focused attacks on limbs or extremities can render them useless, even without destroying them completely. A body part is crippled if it takes damage over a specific threshold in a single attack.

  • Limb (Arm/Leg): Crippled if damage is over 1/2 total HP.
  • Extremity (Hand/Foot): Crippled if damage is over 1/3 total HP.
  • Face: Crippled (blinded) if damage is over 1/10 total HP.

A crippled body part is unusable. The character immediately drops anything held in a crippled hand or arm, and falls prone if a leg or foot is crippled. Crippling hits also carry a high risk of severe bleeding or fluid leaks (see below).

Head & Vitals

Strikes to critical areas are significantly more dangerous, bypassing standard durability and increasing the risk of severe injury.

  • The Head (Skull/Face/Brain):
  • The skull provides natural DR 2.
  • Damage that penetrates the skull is multiplied by x4 (for pi, cr, cut, etc.).
  • Any wound to the head that causes any HP loss after DR requires a HT roll to avoid knockdown and stunning. A Major Wound to the head requires a HT-10 roll.
  • The Vitals (Upper Torso):
  • Attacks targeting the vitals with impaling (imp) or piercing (pi, pi+, pi++) weapons are especially deadly.
  • Damage to the vitals is multiplied by x3 (instead of the usual multiplier for the damage type).
  • A Major Wound to the vitals requires a HT-5 roll to avoid knockdown and stunning.

Bleeding

Severe wounds don’t just stop hurting when the combat ends; they continue to drain a combatant’s life force or system integrity. Organics bleed blood; droids and vehicles leak coolant, lubricants, or hydraulic fluid.

  • The Trigger: Whenever a character suffers a Crippling Injury, they must immediately make a HT roll.
  • Failure: The character begins to bleed (or leak).
  • The Interval: The rate at which you lose vitality or power depends on your activity level:
  • In Combat / Strenuous Activity: Roll HT every 10 seconds (10 turns).
  • Out of Combat / Resting: Roll HT every 1 minute.
  • The Consequences: On a failed HT roll at the end of the interval:
  • Organics: Lose an additional 1 HP due to blood loss.
  • Droids: Lose 5 Power Points (PP) due to coolant loss causing overheating, or hydraulic pump strain.
  • Natural Stopping: Bleeding or leaking stops naturally if the character achieves three consecutive successful HT rolls during their interval checks, or if they roll a Critical Success on any single check.
  • Stabilization: Bleeding can be stopped instantly with a successful First Aid check (for organics) or Mechanic/Armoury check (for droids/cybernetics), or by using an appropriate medpac, repair kit, or Force Healing.

Amputation & Permanent Loss

The violence of the Mandalorian Wars frequently leaves lasting scars. A limb or extremity can be completely severed or destroyed beyond repair.

  • Severing Threshold: If a limb or extremity takes damage equal to or greater than twice the crippling threshold in a single blow from a cutting weapon (like a vibroblade or lightsaber) or a heavy explosive, it is severed.
  • Example: If a character’s total HP is 10, their arm crippling threshold is 5 damage. Taking 10 or more cutting damage to the arm in one hit severs it.
  • Lightsaber Wounds: Because lightsabers cauterize wounds instantly, amputations caused by lightsabers do not trigger bleeding rules, though they still cause Shock and Major Wounds.
  • Cybernetic Replacement: A severed body part is permanently lost and must be replaced by a cybernetic prosthetic if the character wishes to regain its function (see the Cybernetics section below).

When an attacker scores a Critical Hit against a droid, or a single attack inflicts damage that exceeds the droid’s DR by more than a factor of two, the attack causes a localized system failure. Roll 1d6 on the table below in addition to normal damage:

Endurance Points

In combat, Endurance Points (EP) act as a pacing mechanic that forces fighters to manage their stamina. If you swing too hard, wear heavy armor, or fight for too long, you will quickly become too exhausted to defend yourself.

Encumbrance

Armor does not drain EP simply by sitting on your character sheet; it drains EP because its weight shifts your Encumbrance Level.

  • The Formula: At the end of any fight, you pay a flat penalty based on your gear weight relative to your Strength (ST):
  • No Encumbrance (0): Costs 1 EP total.
  • Light (1): Costs 2 EP total.
  • Medium (2): Costs 3 EP total.
  • Heavy (3): Costs 4 EP total.
  • Extra-Heavy (4): Costs 5 EP total.
  • Trained Efficiency: A successful Armor (Light/Medium/Heavy) skill roll (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}) when donning armor of the matching weight class treats your Encumbrance Level as one category lower for this EP cost only -- your actual carried weight, Basic Lift, and Move are unaffected. The roll is made once per donning, and its effect lasts for the day, not per fight. This is the reward for holding the specialty; the cost of lacking it is a flat -1 DX in Medium armor and -2 DX in Heavy, for as long as it is worn (see Armor, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}). Light armor carries no such penalty.
  • The Vicious Cycle: If your EP drops below 1/3 of your maximum, your ST is halved. This instantly drops your carrying capacity, meaning your heavy armor suddenly pushes you into a much worse Encumbrance category, spiking your EP costs even higher for the rest of the day.

Swing Strength (Weapon Minimums and Unreadying)

Unlike some game systems, swinging a sword normally does not cost 1 EP per swing. Instead, GURPS punishes you if your weapon is too heavy for your current strength or requires re-balancing.

  • *Weapon Minimum ST: Every weapon has a minimum ST requirement (e.g., a Greatsword requires ST 12). If your ST matches or exceeds this, swinging it is free.
  • The “Too Heavy” Penalty: If your ST drops below the weapon’s minimum ST (which happens frequently when you hit the 1/3 EP threshold and your ST is halved), you lose 1 EP per swing because you are physically straining to wield it. Furthermore, your weapon skill drops by -1 for every point of ST you lack.
  • Unready Weapons (The EP Cost to Fix): Massive swing weapons like Greataxes or Halberds become “Unready” after you attack. To swing them again next turn, you must take a Ready action. If you don’t want to waste a turn, you can spend 1 EP on a Quick-Ready to instantly ready it. Heavy swing weapons drain your EP pool rapidly if you force them to strike every single turn.

Fight Length (The 10-Second Rule)

GURPS combat turns are incredibly fast, representing exactly 1 second of real time. Because of this, fight length is tracked in 10-second increments.

  • Under 10 Seconds: Most GURPS fights end in 3 to 6 seconds. If the fight is over in less than 10 seconds, you only pay the post-combat encumbrance cost once.
  • Over 10 Seconds: If a battle drags on, you must pay your combat EP cost (1 + Encumbrance) every 10 seconds.
  • The Math: A character in Medium Encumbrance (3 EP cost) fighting a long battle pays:
  • Seconds 1–10: 3 EP
  • Seconds 11–20: Another 3 EP (6 EP total)
  • Seconds 21–30: Another 3 EP (9 EP total)
  • Because most characters only have 10 to 12 EP, a heavily armored fight that lasts just 30 seconds will completely exhaust a normal humanoid, reducing them to a defenseless state.

Running Away and Chasing

If combat turns into a pursuit, sprinting costs 1 EP per 15 seconds of running. This is modified by your Encumbrance level, meaning heavily armored players cannot chase down unarmored ones without quickly collapsing from exhaustion.

Costs After the Fight (Post-Combat Loss)

You do not track EP loss second-by-second during a standard melee brawl. Instead, you calculate the toll once the fight ends.

  • The Core Rule: A battle costs 1 EP plus your Encumbrance Level.
  • Example: If you have Light Encumbrance (1), you lose 2 EP total at the end of the fight.
  • Time Limit: This cost applies to any fight lasting less than 10 seconds. If a fight somehow lasts longer, you pay this cost every 10 seconds (10 combat turns).
